elements.content: Communication Goal: I can talk about my family and use plural nouns.

Lesson overview:
- Level: A0 General English
- Unit: Unit 2. Big happy family
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: It's my family
- Materials: Family-tree template, number cards, plural noun cards, COSYmanuals 'plurals' and 'have got' pages.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• identify core family member vocabulary
• use numbers 1–100 and plural noun endings
Recycling & Course Continuity:

Prior learning: Recycles 'to be', pronouns, and adjectives from Unit 1.

Quick retrieval task: which words or phrases do you remember?
Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (10 items):

mother — a female parent. Example: My mother is a nurse.
father — a male parent. Example: My father works in an office.
parent — a mother or father. Example: My parents live in Cairo.
son — a male child. Example: Their son is ten.
daughter — a female child. Example: Her daughter is a student.
brother — a male sibling. Example: I have one brother.
sister — a female sibling. Example: She has two sisters.
child — a young person. Example: The child is happy.
family — parents, children, and relatives. Example: My family is big.
grandparent — a grandmother or grandfather. Example: My grandparents live in the village.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• This is my mother. (introducing a family member)
• I have one brother and two sisters. (talking about siblings)
• How many children are in your family? (asking about family size)
• We are a big family. (describing family size)
• My grandparents live in... (talking about grandparents)
• These are my parents. (introducing parents)
Vocabulary practice: choose the correct word.
Which word means 'a female parent'?
Which word means 'a male parent'?
Complete the sentence with a word from the list.
Pronunciation Focus: Plural -s endings /s/, /z/, /ɪz/

brothers /ˈbrʌðəz/ — plural /z/
sisters /ˈsɪstəz/ — plural /z/
parents /ˈpeərənts/ — plural /s/
children /ˈtʃɪldrən/ — irregular plural
Listen and repeat:
My brothers are students. My sisters are teachers. These are my parents.

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use plural nouns to talk about more than one person or thing.

Form:
Regular plural nouns: Most nouns add -s: book → books. Nouns ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x add -es: box → boxes. Consonant + y → -ies: city → cities.

Examples:
• one book → two books
• one box → three boxes
• one city → two cities
• one family → two families
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
I have two ___. (sister)
There are three ___ on the table. (box)
We live in two ___. (city)
My ___ are nice. (parent)
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I have two ... (brother / sister / child).
• There are three ... (box / chair / lamp) in the room.
• My ... (friend / cousin) are here.
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• How many brothers and sisters do you have?
• How many chairs are in your kitchen?
• How many books are on your desk?
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write three sentences with plural nouns about your family.
• Write three sentences with plural nouns about your room.
Reading: It's my family

My family is big. I have one brother and two sisters. My brother is a student. My sisters are teachers. My parents are from Egypt. My grandparents live in a small village. We have three children in our home. We are a happy family.
How many sisters does the writer have?
Where do the grandparents live?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: How many people are in your family?
B: There are six people: my parents, my two sisters, my brother, and me.
A: How old is your brother?
B: He is ten. He is a student.
A: And your sisters?
B: They are teachers.
How many people are in the family?
What do the sisters do?
Speaking task: Draw a simple family tree and explain it to your partner. Use numbers and plural nouns.

• How many people are in your family?
• How many brothers and sisters have you got?
• Do your grandparents live near you?
• What is a typical family size in your country?
• Who is the youngest person in your family?
Role-play: You are at a family party. Introduce your family members to a friend and answer questions about them.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write five sentences about your family. Use at least three plural nouns.
Model: My family is ... I have ... My parents are ... My grandparents ... We are ...
